name: Fontaine de Mars
short_description: Napoleonic-era neoclassical fountain at 129 rue Saint-Dominique depicting Mars and Hygeia, built 1806-1809.

beats.script_body: At the arcaded corner of rue Saint-Dominique and rue de l'Exposition stands La Fontaine de Mars, one of several fountains bequeathed to Paris by Napoleon. Mars, god of war, is depicted being offered water by Hygeia, goddess of health. The adjacent restaurant of the same name is one of those unpretentious places with genuine atmosphere — warm, welcoming, and serving honest traditional French cooking, a rarity in modern Paris.
physical_cues: Arcaded hemicycle at the corner; Mars's helmeted head and Hygeia with serpent
beats.source_passage: La Fontaine de Mars, one of several bequeathed to Paris by Napoleon. Mars, the god of war, is depicted being offered water by the goddess of health, Hygeia.

opening_hours_basis: A street fountain viewed from the open pavement; not gated.
visit_basis: Neoclassical Napoleonic-era fountain with a relief of Mars and Hygeia set into a street corner; a freestanding monument you view and walk around, nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A street-side fountain on a narrow pavement gives no traffic-free running room and no real free seating, but rue Saint-Dominique is a lit, populated street after dark.
queue_basis: An open street fountain with no interior and no door; the whole value stands in the open, so there is nothing to queue for.

name: Église Saint-Pierre du Gros Caillou
short_description: Parish church at 92 rue Saint-Dominique, the 1822 successor to the original village church of the Gros Caillou neighbourhood.
name_variations: Church of Saint-Pierre du Gros Caillou

beats.script_body: West of the Invalides was once a village called Le Gros Caillou — 'the big stone' — named after the boundary marker between the domains of the abbeys of Saint-Germain and Sainte-Geneviève. The village grew up to serve the 30-year construction of the Invalides: its first shop was a butcher's on rue Saint-Dominique, and the parallel rue de Grenelle accommodated laundresses who did the Invalides' washing in the Seine. Its parish church at n° 92 rue Saint-Dominique was won only after years of petitions to the King — before it, villagers had to drag all the way to Saint-Sulpice for their sacraments. The current church dates from 1822.
physical_cues: Plain 19th-century facade at 92 rue Saint-Dominique
beats.source_passage: The church of Saint-Pierre du Gros Caillou at n° 92 was the original parish church of the long-forgotten village.

opening_hours_basis: A parish church you enter; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Modest 1822 neoclassical parish church on a market street; a plain single-nave interior with side altars, about 15 minutes to walk through with no queue.
judgement_basis: A parish church where quiet rules out running and which offers no free public seating, but it fronts the lit and busy rue Saint-Dominique where people pass at night.
queue_basis: A parish church with an open door and free entry walked straight into; no ticket desk or screening creates a line.

name: Rue Cler
short_description: Pedestrianised market street in the 7th arrondissement, celebrated for its village atmosphere and daily produce market.

beats.script_body: More than any other street, pedestrian rue Cler perpetuates the village atmosphere of the old Gros Caillou neighbourhood. Its permanent market — held both mornings and afternoons — is described as the most picturesque street in the 7th arrondissement: an explosion of genuine local colour, all the more vivid for being such a contrast with the formal residential avenues surrounding it.
physical_cues: Cobblestones and market stalls between rue de Grenelle and avenue de la Motte-Picquet
beats.source_passage: the pedestrian rue Cler... perpetuates the village atmosphere par excellence with its permanent market.

opening_hours_basis: An open pedestrian market street whose value stands in the open; not gated.
visit_basis: Pedestrianised market street lined with produce stalls, cheesemongers, cafés and shopfronts; its whole value is strolling its length and pausing at displays, which easily absorbs twenty minutes.
judgement_basis: A pedestrianised market street free of through-traffic still crowds with shoppers, stalls and café tables that leave no clear running room and only paid seating, but it is lit and peopled into the evening.
queue_basis: A pedestrian market street with no door or gate; the whole experience is in the open air with nothing to enter.

name: Ecole Militaire
short_description: 18th-century military academy on Avenue de la Motte-Picquet, commissioned by Louis XV with Madame de Pompadour's backing and designed by Gabriel.

beats.script_body: Just as Madame de Maintenon founded the school of Saint-Cyr for the children of the impoverished nobility, Madame de Pompadour founded the École Militaire to enable impoverished young men to become officers. She instructed Gabriel — who had already impressed the court with his Petit Trianon at Versailles — to design this new academy. Among the cadets who later paraded on the adjacent Champ de Mars was a poor Corsican who would one day inspect and distribute honours to the troops there.
physical_cues: Grand classical façade facing Place de Fontenoy
Central pavilion with Corinthian columns
beats.source_passage: Madame de Pompadour founded the Ecole Militaire to enable impoverished young men to become officers... instructed Gabriel.

opening_hours_basis: An active military academy behind walls, not generally open to visitors; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Monumental 18th-century military academy by Gabriel with a domed central pavilion and long facade facing the Champ de Mars; still an active military school, so viewed from the parade-ground front and forecourt, no public interior.
judgement_basis: A working military academy behind gates and fences offers no accessible interior run-space or free seating, but it sits on the wide lit Avenue de la Motte-Picquet with traffic and passers-by at night.
queue_basis: A working military academy closed to general public entry and viewed from the exterior; there is no visitor line.

name: UNESCO Headquarters Paris
short_description: UNESCO's Paris headquarters at Place de Fontenoy, a Y-shaped Modernist building (1958) by Breuer, Nervi, and Zehrfuss, with a Japanese garden by Isamu Noguchi.

beats.script_body: On Place de Fontenoy, facing the west wing of the École Militaire, stands the UNESCO building, designed jointly by Marcel Breuer (US), Pier Luigi Nervi (Italy) and Bernard Zehrfuss (France), and inaugurated in 1958. Its Y-shaped form was quite revolutionary when it was designed, and, like all good architecture, remains effective today. Outside stand works by Calder, Miró, and Moore; inside, by Picasso, Arp, Braque, Miró, and others. The Japanese garden was designed by the sculptor Isamu Noguchi, who returned to Paris to restore it in 1988, shortly before his death.
physical_cues: Y-shaped concrete structure visible from Place de Fontenoy
beats.source_passage: the UNESCO building, designed jointly by Marcel Breuer (US), Pietro Nervi (Italy) and Bernard Zehrfuss (France).

opening_hours_basis: A headquarters building entered only by prior arrangement/guided visit; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Y-shaped 1958 Modernist building with sculptures and a Noguchi Japanese garden; the exterior, forecourt art and garden fill about twelve minutes, and interior access requires arranged visits rather than casual entry.
judgement_basis: A secured institutional building with a private Noguchi garden inaccessible without entry offers no public run-space or free seating, and its Place de Fontenoy frontage is quiet and unwelcoming for lingering after dark.
queue_basis: Public access requires advance registration and passes an airport-style security check at the gate, but visitor volume is low, so the screening line stays minor even at its busiest.

name: Champ de Mars
short_description: Large public greenspace flanking the Eiffel Tower, formerly the parade ground of the Ecole Militaire and site of successive Expositions Universelles.

beats.script_body: The Champ de Mars was the stage for the earliest experiments in flight. On 27 August 1783, the physicist J. A. C. Charles and the Robert brothers released the world's first unmanned hydrogen balloon from here — a 35-cubic-metre sphere of rubberised silk that flew 15 miles in three-quarters of an hour. The people of Gonesse, east of Paris, were panic-stricken when it descended on them from the heavens. Then on 2 March 1784, Jean-Pierre Blanchard brought his sophisticated balloon equipped with four oars and a rudder — it was meant to float northeast to La Villette but headed stubbornly west to Billancourt, to the delight of the chansonniers. Undaunted, Blanchard went on to make the first aerial crossing of the English Channel from Dover to Calais in January 1785, together with American John Jeffries.
physical_cues: Flat open field — original launchpad for ballooning
beats.source_passage: on 27 August, the Roberts released this first unmanned hydrogen balloon from the Champ-de-Mars.

beats.script_body: In 1863 the photographer Nadar took off from the Champ de Mars in a huge balloon called Le Géant, accompanied by prominent figures, in a nacelle styled as a two-storey wicker house. On his second flight the balloon crashed in Hanover, Germany, injuring Nadar.
physical_cues: Site of Le Géant's first launch on 4 October 1863
beats.source_passage: In 1863 the photographer Nadar took off from the Champ-de-Mars... in a huge balloon with a double-decker nacelle, called Le Géant.

beats.script_body: The authorities of the Revolution chose the Champ de Mars as the site for the first Bastille Day celebrations — La Fête de la Fédération — on 14 July 1790, presided over by Talleyrand. 300,000 fervent patriots, including the Royal Family, gathered here; La Fayette, standing in the pouring rain, took the Nation's oath, the first citizen to do so. By 1793 the Terror had arrived: the guillotine was briefly erected here to execute the hated Bailly — former President of the Constituent Assembly and Mayor of Paris — who waited stoically while the blood-thirsty crowd covered him in spittle and mud.
physical_cues: Vast open axis from Ecole Militaire to Eiffel Tower
beats.source_passage: 300,000 fervent patriots - including the Royal Family - were convened here on that 14 July 1790.

beats.script_body: From 1855 the Champ de Mars became the playground of the emerging capitalist age — the site of successive Expositions Universelles where French technological achievements dazzled the world. The 1889 fair featured the Galerie des Machines (420 × 115 metres, 16,000 machines) and the just-completed Eiffel Tower rising 300 metres — never before had mortal eye embraced such horizons except from a balloon. In 1900, an electrically operated moving wooden platform transported visitors from the Champ de Mars to the Champs-Élysées and back, electricity still being a luxury. The age of Universal Exhibitions has gone, an ephemeral spark fizzled out by ennui before being swept away by universal cataclysms.
physical_cues: Vast plain that hosted temporary exhibition halls
beats.source_passage: in 1855 the Champ-de-Mars was singled out to become the gigantic playground of the emerging capitalist society.

beats.script_body: An event of great novelty occurred on the Champ de Mars one fine morning in 1780: two gentlemen ran a horse-race for a bet, the first of a series of sports imported from England that became fashionable in Paris throughout the 19th century. Marie-Antoinette gave enthusiastic support; even the Revolution adopted horse-racing, though the jockeys of those 'patriotic horse-races of public utility' wore tricoloured sashes. The Champ de Mars remained Paris's racecourse until 1855, when Longchamp in the Bois de Boulogne took over.
physical_cues: Long flat expanse — nearly 800m from Ecole Militaire to Eiffel Tower
beats.source_passage: An event of great novelty occurred here one fine morning in 1780, when two gentlemen ran in a horse-race for a bet.

opening_hours_basis: An open public greenspace whose value stands in the open; OSM tag '24/7' confirms it is not gated.
visit_basis: Vast formal greenspace stretching from the Ecole Militaire to the Eiffel Tower, with long tree-lined lawns and walks between viewpoints; crossing it and pausing for the tower view absorbs over half an hour.
judgement_basis: A vast traffic-free lawn lets children run loud and free with benches and grass for quiet conversation, but the open park is unlit in stretches, sees crowds thin at night and is periodically fenced near the Tower.
queue_basis: An open public greensward with no gate or ticket; visitors walk on freely from any side.

anchors.label: The central lawn
anchors.basis: The long axis of lawn between the tree lines is where the Revolution's festivals were staged and where a person stands back to look at the tower framed by the park. Half the footprint: you take the lawn in from anywhere along its middle, not from one blade of grass.

name: Les Invalides
short_description: 17th-century military complex containing Napoleon's tomb beneath a gilded dome and the Army Museum with 500,000 artefacts

beats.script_body: The church of the Dome — also known as the Royal Chapel — is one of the most outstanding monuments in Paris, a masterpiece of 17th-century architecture built by Jules-Hardouin Mansart. Its proportions were once seen at their best from Avenue de Breteuil on a fine morning, when the deep purple dome looked almost palpably mellow and pulpy. That patina was lost when Paris was groomed for the bicentenary of the Revolution: the dome was daubed with shiny gold paint. The regilding was executed to the highest standards, but it destroyed what only time can bestow. By night, however, the dome shimmering against the dark sky above the floodlit walls remains enchanting.
physical_cues: Look up at the golden dome
Best appreciated from Place Vauban or Pont Alexandre III
beats.source_passage: the church of the Dome (also known as the Royal Chapel)... a masterpiece of 17th-century architecture, built by Jules-Hardouin Mansart.

beats.script_body: It was Louis XIV, assisted by his minister Louvois, who in 1670 founded the Hôtel des Invalides. Distressed by the sight of war cripples reduced to begging on the Pont-Neuf after loyal service on the battlefield, the Sun King felt he owed them respectable shelter. The initiative had earlier roots: Henri IV in 1604 had provided shelter for veterans on the present rue Broca, and Louis XIII and Richelieu built the hospital of Bicêtre. But Louis XIV tackled the issue on a grand scale, commissioning Libéral Bruant to build a monument colossal in size — its façade measures 195 metres across and the main courtyard, the Cour d'Honneur, 102 metres by 63 — yet subdued in character. Montesquieu wrote of it: 'I believe this to be the most respectable place on earth.'
physical_cues: Façade stretches 195m across
Cour d'Honneur 102m by 63m
beats.source_passage: it was Louis XIV, assisted by his minister Louvois, who in 1670 founded the Hotel des Invalides.

beats.script_body: The veterans Louis XIV sheltered here were not easily persuaded to trade their scrappy independence on the Pont-Neuf for military discipline. And they had good reason to be alarmed: infractions were punished by anything from deprivation of wine to imprisonment, or by public humiliation astride a wooden horse. If caught with a woman of pleasure, both were exposed together for the amusement of passers-by. A complaint about poor soup once sparked a full-blown riot. Minister Louvois crushed the rebellion and had the most unruly rebel shot by a firing squad.
physical_cues: Cour d'Honneur where punishments were displayed
beats.source_passage: a harsh military discipline was imposed... a complaint about the poor quality of the soup sparked off an outburst of violence, which soon developed into a full-blown riot.

beats.script_body: Louvois was not a modest man and had his eye on the Invalides as his own sepulchre. Louis XIV would not tolerate such impertinence and had his remains removed elsewhere. But Louvois did find a subtle way to perpetuate his name: as you enter the Cour d'Honneur, look at the fifth garret to the right of the left-hand pavilion. Its bull's-eye window is framed by a wolf ('loup') that gazes ('voit') intensely down on the courtyard — a far-fetched pun, but one that passed unnoticed by the Sun King.
physical_cues: Fifth garret right of left-hand pavilion in Cour d'Honneur — bull's-eye window framed by carved wolf
beats.source_passage: look at the fifth garret to the right of the left-hand side pavilion; its bull's-eye window is framed by a wolf ('loup') which looks ('voit') intensely down on to the courtyard.

beats.script_body: Napoleon wished to be buried 'on the banks of the Seine, by the French people whom I have loved so much.' After seven years of negotiations with the English, his ashes arrived from Saint Helena on 15 December 1840, travelling via Le Havre, up the Seine to Pont de Neuilly, then down the Champs-Élysées to the Invalides through a snowstorm. Victor Hugo, who was present, described the moment the sun broke through as the hearse appeared: 'The effect was prodigious indeed.' Some 850,000 Parisians came to pay homage in the following days. Napoleon's ashes were finally moved to their permanent tomb — designed by Visconti — on 2 April 1861. He lies within six nested coffins; a silver vase holds his heart; a silver box, his stomach.
physical_cues: Circular crypt with massive red quartzite sarcophagus
Twelve allegorical figures around the tomb
beats.source_passage: the Emperor's ashes were brought from the island of Saint Helena to the Invalides on the 15 December 1840.

beats.script_body: The church of Saint-Louis-des-Invalides — the original church of the institution, designed by Libéral Bruant — boasts a magnificent 17th-century organ. It was here, on 5 December 1837, that Hector Berlioz's Requiem received its world premiere, performed with 188 instrumentalists and 210 choristers, at a ceremony commemorating General Damrémont, killed at the Siege of Constantine.
physical_cues: 17th-century organ inside Saint-Louis-des-Invalides
beats.source_passage: The church also boasts a magnificent 17th-century organ which was used in 1837, for the first performance of Berlioz's Requiem.

beats.script_body: Buried in the crypt of Saint-Louis-des-Invalides is Rouget de Lisle, the captain from Strasbourg who in 1792 composed 'Le Chant de guerre pour l'armée du Rhin' — the song that became La Marseillaise, France's ferociously sanguinary national anthem. His ashes were brought here on 14 July 1915, awaiting a planned transfer to the Panthéon that has never yet happened.
physical_cues: Governors' Crypt of Saint-Louis-des-Invalides
beats.source_passage: Rouget de Lisle, the captain from Strasbourg who in 1792 composed Le Chant de guerre pour l'armée du Rhin... His ashes were brought here on 14 July 1915.

beats.script_body: Napoleon was determined to stamp his own identity on the Invalides and eclipse his predecessor. In 1797 he transferred the lion of the defeated Serenissima Republic to this stronghold of French military glory, placing it atop a fountain in the centre of the Esplanade. He also hoped to bring the golden cross of the Kremlin back as a trophy and display it on the Dome — but history decided otherwise. The Venetian lion's Parisian career was brief: by 1815 it had returned to its column in Piazza San Marco.
physical_cues: Central fountain on the Esplanade des Invalides
beats.source_passage: in 1797, had already transferred the lion of the defeated Serenissima Republic to this stronghold of France's military glory.

opening_hours_basis: Gated museum and tomb complex; hours from the Army Museum's own published daily opening pattern.
visit_basis: The vast forecourt, the cannon line and the gilded dome seen from the esplanade absorb 25 minutes; inside are Napoleon's tomb beneath the dome and the huge Army Museum, which would absorb over two hours, capped at the 90-minute tour maximum plus a ticket queue.
judgement_basis: The museum and tomb interiors are hushed and gated, but the vast open lawns of the Esplanade des Invalides are traffic-free with grass and benches where people sit and talk; the esplanade is lit and reasonably trafficked, so standing after dark is acceptable, though the lawns are large and open rather than fully enclosed which combined with bordering roads keeps children_can_run false.
queue_basis: The wide complex has a ticket desk and light bag check for Napoleon's tomb and the Army Museum, producing only a minor midday line that clears early or late.

name: 29 Avenue Rapp
short_description: Award-winning 1901 Art Nouveau apartment building by Jules Lavirotte with fantastically ornate carvings of flora, fauna, and Adam and Eve

beats.script_body: At n° 29 Avenue Rapp stands an astonishing building by Jules Lavirotte, built in 1901 and frequently compared to the work of Antoni Gaudí. It is one of the finest surviving examples of Art Nouveau in Paris, its façade lavished with ceramic sculpture — flowers, animals, bison heads supporting balconies, fox-headed fur collars — and awarded the prize for the most original new façade in the 7th arrondissement that year.
physical_cues: Ceramic facade
Extraordinary sculpted entrance door frame
beats.source_passage: At n° 29 is an astonishing building, built by Lavirotte and extremely reminiscent of the work of the Spanish architect, Gaudf.

opening_hours_basis: Art Nouveau building facade admired from the street (walk-by only), no admission gate, so not gated.
visit_basis: A single ornate 1901 Art Nouveau facade dense with carvings and a famous doorway; an engaged visitor spends around twelve minutes tracing the detail, with no public interior.
judgement_basis: A walk-by facade on a pavement beside a busy avenue with no seating and no room to run safely, but the avenue is central, lit and trafficked into the evening.
queue_basis: An ornate apartment facade admired from the pavement with no public interior, so there is no queue to enter.

name: Eiffel Tower
short_description: Iron lattice tower built by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 World Fair, standing 330 metres tall on the Champ de Mars

beats.script_body: How ironic to recall that 300 prominent members of the intelligentsia signed a petition against the Eiffel Tower's erection, calling it a crime against history and against Paris. Yet it survived its planned demolition and became the unassailable emblem of the city. Even visitors familiar with skyscrapers feel overwhelmed as they approach it: 18,038 metal pieces held together by 2.5 million rivets weighing 7,300 tonnes — an extraordinary technological feat.
physical_cues: Lattice of iron visible in daylight
beats.source_passage: 300 prominent members of the intelligentsia of the time signed a petition against its erection.

beats.script_body: The Tower has attracted both the heroic and the desperate. Eccentrics attempted to fly from it with homemade wings — an Austrian called Reichelt in 1912 hit the ground head first. In 1977 a French stunt man flew a hang-glider from the first floor; an English couple parachuted from the third; an American pilot flew between its legs and lost his licence. Of the 380 people who have hurled themselves from the Tower, only one escaped death — a young woman in 1964 who landed on the roof of a parked car. That year suicides averaged one per month, after which parapets were installed.
physical_cues: Safety parapets and mesh added after 1964
beats.source_passage: Of the 380 people who have hurled themselves from the Tower, only one escaped death - a young woman who in 1964 jumped from the first floor but landed on the roof of a parked car.

beats.script_body: During World War I, the Eiffel Tower played a crucial military role: Mata Hari, the infamous dancer-spy, was identified through radio transmissions intercepted at the Tower's wireless station. Coded messages sent by a German contact referred to agent 'H21' — swiftly identified as Mata Hari. She was captured and shot on 15 October 1917. Nearly 50,000 words were received and transmitted from the Tower during that war — alone a compelling reason not to demolish it.
physical_cues: Antenna at the summit — descendant of WWI radio mast
beats.source_passage: Identified through its radio transmissions as H21, she was captured and shot on 15 October 1917.

opening_hours_basis: Gated ticketed monument with elevator/stair access; hours follow the tower's own published year-round daily pattern (extended summer hours from mid-June).
visit_basis: The Champ de Mars and the space beneath the four piers absorb over half an hour of looking up and photographing; going up involves long security and lift queues plus two viewing levels and the summit, which would absorb well over two hours, capped at the 90-minute tour maximum.
judgement_basis: The Champ de Mars lawns run traffic-free but the immediate base is a fenced, security-controlled paved plaza crossed by roads and crowds where a child at speed can reach traffic and there is no quiet free seating; the site is brightly lit and busy with people at all hours, so a person left standing at night would be fine.
queue_basis: Airport-style security screening at the base perimeter plus separate lift-ticket lines feed a small number of elevators, so even timed tickets leave a substantial wait that worsens in summer midday, dropping only near opening or late evening.

anchors.label: The base
anchors.basis: The esplanade under the four feet is where the queues form and where a person stands to look straight up through the lattice; the corpus's queue and security lines are about this esplanade. Half the footprint, as a place you look at demands.
